statement: SPRAT is a collaborative workbench for aligning web-system requirements with privacy and security policies.
evidence_summary: [initial_requirement:INITIAL_REQUIREMENTS] Requirements and privacy analysts need SPRAT, a collaborative workbench for aligning web-system requirements with privacy and security policies. Users should be able to capture goals, scenarios, policies, requirements, and legal-compliance information; trace goals back to their source policies; organize them with flexible classifications; and compare analyses produced by different people. Access should vary for administrators, project managers, analysts, and guests.; [interview_turn:T002] Yes, this tool is meant to help analysts work together on web-system requirements and make sure those requirements line up with privacy and security policies from the start. Right now, a lot of that work is spread across documents, spreadsheets, and emails, so people lose traceability and it becomes hard to compare what different analysts concluded. We want SPRAT to centralize the goals, scenarios, policies, requirements, and compliance notes in one place so the team can reason about them consistently.

statement: The system shall support a controlled vocabulary or shared glossary.
evidence_summary: [interview_turn:T014] We do have some shared terms, but they’re not managed very consistently today, so people sometimes use slightly different wording for the same concept. I would definitely want SPRAT to support a controlled vocabulary or at least a shared glossary, because that would make the analyses easier to compare and reduce ambiguity. It would also help if the tool could reuse approved terms when people are entering goals, policies, and requirements.; [interview_turn:T018] Yes, the biggest issue is that people can describe the same thing in different ways, or use the same term to mean slightly different things, which leads to mismatched traces and extra rework later. SPRAT could help by keeping a shared glossary, showing accepted definitions when someone enters a term, and warning when a new term is too close to an existing one or is being used inconsistently. That kind of support would make reviews faster and reduce mistakes in the analysis.
